transcript:
Meeting header:
Title: Verdigris Labs weekly pilot econ tuning + handoff
Date/Time: 2026-06-05 14:30 PT
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Verdigris ML Eng), Maya Ortiz (Verdigris CTO), Samir Patel (Verdigris Infra)

Summary:
Quick sync to review latest token/unit economics from the pilot, go over caching and batching observations, and align on handoff plan for the 2-week dedicated benchmark. Emphasis on tokens/sec/$, where caching is delivering savings, and tradeoffs to accept for tail latency.

Topics discussed:
- Current pilot results: tokens per dollar and per-second throughput
- Caching effectiveness for prefix reuse and KV cache hit rates
- Batching tradeoffs: latency P95 vs throughput gains
- Model variants and quantization impact on unit cost
- Private vs hosted routing for compliance-sensitive requests
- Next steps and ownership for benchmark and security artifacts

Action items (as captured verbally):
- Alex will re-run pricing model with new sequence length histogram and share spreadsheet
- Priya will run an isolated throughput sweep across 4 model configs and upload results to the shared folder
- Verdigris to share the 7-day prompt corpus and traffic mix
- Schedule 2-hour dedicated benchmark window next week

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Carter: All right, thanks everyone for joining. Quick check-in, we wanted to go over last week's pilot numbers and then lay out the handoff for the dedicated run. Priya, you want to kick with the numbers?
[00:18] Priya Nair: Sure. So summary first — across the pilot we've observed about 9,800 tokens per dollar on hosted medium configs when we include streaming overhead. That is averaged across short and medium prompts; longer sequences drop the tokens-per-dollar down to roughly 6k because of kv cache misses we still see.
[00:35] Jordan Lee: Sorry, can you repeat — 9,800 tokens per dollar is the average across what baseline? Are you including pre- and post-processing?
[00:44] Priya Nair: Good call. It's model output tokens only, not counting our front-end formatting. We can easily add a line to include end-to-end. For the pilot's traffic mix — 60% sub-128 tokens, 30% 128-512, 10% >512.
[01:05] Samir Patel: That 10% long tail is where we see spikes in latency, yeah. The KV case — sorry, kv cache — misses are correlating with those longer sessions, so the caching savings drop there.
[01:18] Priya Nair: Right. When we use prefix caching on repeated system prompts we've seen hit rates of about 35-42% which reduced token spend by roughly 28% on applicable requests. That translated to a 20% uplift in tokens/sec/$ for routes that are cache-friendly.
[01:40] Maya Ortiz: That's helpful. On the quantization front, you mentioned a 15% additional cost reduction if we moved to 4-bit quantized variants. What's the tradeoff on quality?
[01:53] Priya Nair: Our evals showed small drop in F1 on the reranking tasks — like 1.5 to 2 points — and occasional jitter on numeric extraction. For customer-facing extraction pipelines that might be risky. So recommend enabling quantized models for lower criticality routes and keep fp16 for the handful of strict extraction endpoints.
[02:14] Jordan Lee: Can you also summarize the batching effects? We tried increasing batch size from 8 to 32 in the pilot cluster and throughput jumped almost 2.8x but p95 latency went from 180ms to about 520ms for those stacked requests. For our UX we need sub-300ms for interactive flows.
[02:37] Priya Nair: Exactly — batching gives you tokens/sec/$ improvements but at the cost of tail latency. Redwood's continuous batching knobs allow dynamic caps; we can keep a per-route latency cap and the runtime will trade off batch size. For interactive routes we recommend a small max batch (8-12) and aggressive prefetching. For asynchronous bulk jobs, push batch up to 32+.
[03:02] Alex Carter: Jordan, what's priority for you — cost or latency? We should align that to pick the config for the dedicated run.
[03:11] Jordan Lee: Latency is priority for the customer-facing search assistant, cost is more important for the analytics batch jobs. So two lane approach makes sense.
[03:19] Maya Ortiz: On the compliance side we need to confirm encryption at rest with our KMS and audit logs. We need to see the private deployment notes. Are you able to support SSO — S M L — SAML?
[03:31] Alex Carter: Yes, Redwood supports SAML SSO and we can provide the SOC2 + ISO packet. For private control plane we have an option that plugs into customer KMS and forwards audit logs to your splunk — or we can set up an S3 sink for a retention window. Priya, can we confirm the KMS integration steps?
[03:47] Priya Nair: Yep — we'll send the KMS integration doc. There's a minor caveat for on-prem HSMs where we need a small connector component, we'll note that in the packet.
[03:57] Samir Patel: For the dedicated run, network egress will be a factor. If we run in our VPC we need to make sure the routing overhead doesn't kill the p50.
[04:07] Priya Nair: We observed about 6-8ms extra per request when routing through a private peering link in the pilot. That was on us-east1 egress; might be different in your colo. We'll measure that in the benchmark.
[04:20] Alex Carter: Let's talk about the concrete handoff. We propose a 2-hour dedicated benchmark window next Wednesday where Redwood will run four configs: hosted fp16 baseline, hosted 4-bit quantized, dedicated reserved pool fp16, and dedicated quantized. We'll sweep batch sizes and measure tokens/sec/$, p50/p95 latencies, and KV hit amplification. Priya to run automation and Jordan to coordinate VPC access.
[04:47] Jordan Lee: That works. One ask — can we get a cost projection that shows tokens/sec/$ at 10k, 100k, and 1M monthly token volumes? The earlier sheet had only 50k and 500k slices.
[04:59] Alex Carter: Sure, we'll extend the model. We'll also add route-level examples so you can see per-endpoint economics.
[05:06] Maya Ortiz: For success criteria, I want to see: 1) user-facing flows <300ms p95 at expected peak load, 2) tokens/sec/$ > 10k for cache-friendly routes, and 3) clear plan to keep sensitive documents inside our VPC for auditability.
[05:22] Priya Nair: Noted. We'll instrument the benchmark to generate the p95 and tokens/sec/$ numbers and attach the raw logs. For the KV cache we're going to run three cache policies so you can see hit curves.
[05:34] Samir Patel: Also want to validate fallback behavior. If dedicated capacity is saturated, what happens — do requests automatically route to hosted with masked PII? We need the routing policy doc.
[05:45] Alex Carter: Redwood's smart routing supports fallbacks and we can configure a policy to route less-sensitive or aggregated requests to hosted. We'll share the routing policy examples.
[05:55] Priya Nair: Small note on measurement noise — streaming clients produced slightly lower tokens/sec/$ in our lab because of chunking inefficiencies. For the dedicated run we suggest using full-response batch pulls to avoid that artifact.
[06:10] Jordan Lee: Good catch. We'll provide how our client streams currently work so you can mimic it.
[06:18] Maya Ortiz: Anything else on security posture? We want to see the audit log retention options and role-based access controls.
[06:24] Alex Carter: We'll include RBAC mapping examples and a default 90-day retention with options to extend.
[06:30] Priya Nair: Back to economics — larger quantized pools dropped cost per token by about 18% in our numbers but again quality tradeoffs are non-linear. For rerank and NER we saw small deltas but for summarization there were occasional degenerate compressions; we'll flag those tests in the report.
[06:52] Jordan Lee: So final question — after the benchmark do we expect to convert to a 3-month reserved pilot?
[07:00] Alex Carter: Likely yes if results meet the thresholds. We'll propose an interim reserved plan and show projected savings across volumes.
[07:07] Maya Ortiz: OK, next steps recap?
[07:10] Alex Carter: Alex: send revised cost model and per-route example by Monday. Priya: schedule and run dedicated benchmark, upload results. Verdigris: provide prompt corpus and confirm access. Redwood: share SOC2/KMS docs and routing policy examples.
[07:25] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Appreciate the thoroughness.
[07:29] Samir Patel: Thanks all, we'll get the prompt set to you by EOD Monday.
[07:33] Alex Carter: Great, we'll follow up on calendar invites. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
